summary: This document describes JSON data structures that represent registration information held by Regional Internet Registries and Domain Name Registries, used to form Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) responses. It was replaced by RFC 9083.

eli5.summary: When you ask who owns a domain, the answer comes in a tidy format that computers can read. This defines that format. It was replaced by RFC 9083.

subtitle: JSON data structures for representing registration information in RDAP queries.

tldr.problem: Domain registries and IP registries needed a way to return structured registration data to queries about domain names, IP addresses, and other resources. The old WHOIS protocol provided only plain text.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines JSON object classes representing entities (people and organizations), nameservers, domains, IP networks, and autonomous system numbers, along with common data structures for events, status, links, and contact information.
tldr.outcome: RDAP servers can now return rich, machine-readable registration data in JSON format. It was replaced by RFC 9083, which provides an updated version.

today: RFC 7483 is a Proposed Standard that defines RDAP JSON response format. It was superseded by RFC 9083, which provides an updated version of the same specification.

sections.title: RDAP and Registration Data
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) is a protocol for querying registration information maintained by Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), such as ARIN and RIPE, and by Domain Name Registries (DNRs), the organizations that manage top-level domains. This RFC describes how RDAP servers send responses in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) format.

RDAP replaces the older WHOIS protocol, which returned only plain text. JSON responses allow clients to parse and understand the data structure automatically. Queries can be for domains, nameservers, IP networks, autonomous system numbers, and entities (people and organizations).
sections.eli5: RDAP is like a librarian who answers questions about who owns a domain or IP address. This document tells the librarian how to write the answers in a tidy format so computers can understand them.

sections.title: Object Classes and Data Structures
sections.content:
RDAP responses use five main object classes, each representing a type of registered resource. Entity objects represent people, organizations, registrars, and other parties. Nameserver objects describe DNS servers used for domain delegation. Domain objects represent DNS domain names with information about their nameservers, contacts, and security settings. IP Network objects represent blocks of IPv4 or IPv6 addresses registered with an RIR, and Autonomous System Number objects represent registered AS numbers.

All objects share common data structures: links reference related resources with relationship types like "self" and "up"; events record actions such as registration and last change with dates; status arrays indicate object state (active, locked, transfer prohibited); and entities can be embedded within other objects to show relationships.
sections.eli5: There are five kinds of things RDAP talks about: people, nameservers, domains, IP addresses, and network numbers. Each kind has information about who touched it and when, and who is in charge of it.

sections.title: Contact Information and Domain Details
sections.content:
Entity objects use jCard, the JSON format of vCard, to represent contact information. A single entity can have multiple email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, and language preferences, each marked with a type and preference order. Postal addresses can be represented either in a structured format (split into components like street, city, and country) or unstructured (a free-form label with newlines).

Domain objects may include variants, representing the same domain in different scripts or with different internationalized domain name (IDN) encoding. For secure domains using DNSSEC, the secureDNS member includes delegation signer (DS) records or key data, allowing clients to verify the chain of trust without separate DNS queries.
sections.eli5: Contact information stores names, emails, phone numbers, and addresses. Domains can have variations spelled different ways, and they can publish encryption keys so people can verify they really own them.

sections.title: Query Responses and Privacy Controls
sections.content:
Responses to lookup queries return a single object (domain, entity, IP network, etc.), while search queries return an array of matching objects. Both types of responses may be truncated due to authorization limits or server load, signaled with typed notices or remarks explaining why data was withheld. Error responses include an HTTP status code, title, and description.

Privacy mechanisms are built into the specification via status values: private marks data that should not be shared without authorization, removed indicates data has been collected but omitted from the response, and obscured means data has been altered (for example, a phone number shown as "XXXX"). These allow registries to protect sensitive contact information while still providing useful registration data.
sections.eli5: When you ask a question, you get back either one answer or many answers. If there is a lot of data, some might be hidden for privacy or to protect from overload. The answer says why if something is missing.

sections.title: Internationalization and Security
sections.content:
RDAP responses support internationalization through UTF-8 encoding (required for all servers and clients), language tags marking text in specific languages, and separate representations of internationalized domain names in both ASCII-compatible encoding (LDH form) and Unicode form. This allows the protocol to serve global registries with multi-script domain names.

Security considerations include protection against code injection in JSON parsing, cache poisoning prevention for clients that cache responses, and privacy protections for sensitive registration data. Servers should follow security requirements in related RDAP specifications and be aware that service operators have responsibility to implement appropriate privacy policies.
sections.eli5: The format works for any language and can show domain names in Chinese, Arabic, or any other script. Servers and clients must be careful not to let bad data sneak in through the JSON, and they should not blindly trust cached answers.
